newsitem.title: CANADA: GM ready to recognize outsourcing limits-CAW.
newsitem.headline: GM ready to recognize outsourcing limits-CAW.

text.p: General Motors Corp is prepared for the first time to recognize limits on the amount of work which can be contracted out, or outsourced, Canadian Auto Workers union president Buzz Hargrove said on Wednesday.
"They are now prepared to recognize that they are going to leave this bargaining table with limits (on outsourcing)," Hargrove told about 160 striking workers occupying a fabrication plant in Oshawa.
Hargrove said this had emerged from a meeting he held with GM's chief executive Jack Smith in Toronto this morning.
In return, Hargrove said, the union is ready to agree that GM is in a different financial position to that of the other two big North American automakers, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp.
"The union is prepared to recognize that they (GM) are different," Hargrove said.

Reporters inside the Oshawa plant where workers were holding a sit-in to prevent GM from moving out key machinery used in component production heard Hargrove promise that negotiations with GM would be resumed at local levels almost immediately. High-level negotiations will resume on Friday.
The workers occupied the plant earlier today after learning that GM Canada was seeking a court injunction to move the machinery in an effort to maintain supply to customers in the United States.
Hargrove said that GM had now agreed to drop the court injunction if the strikers leave the plant.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low confirmed that an agreement had been reached to drop the injuction.
"We will not go forward with the injunction if the workers leave the plant," said Low.
Low declined to comment on the agreement on outsourcing but confirmed that negotiations between the two sides will resume.
"The dialogue today was positive, but there's still a lot of work that needs to be done in order to reach a settlement," said Low.
"There's a commitment by GM and the CAW to get back at the table and drive towards a settlement."
Hargrove said the two sides are going to go back to serious talks with the goal of brokering a deal by 1200 EDT/1600 GMT on Monday.

Hundreds of workers gathered outside the Oshawa plant as Hargrove spoke to about 160 workers inside, on the roof and in the periphery. The strikers chanted and waved banners in support of the union leader.
"If Jack Smith and Buzz made no headway today, we're going to be here for a long time," said Chris Buckley, a local union negotiator.

Talks between the two sides have floundered since the strike began at about midnight October 2. GM had refused to agree to the outsourcing limits laid out in the pattern contract reached by Chrysler and the CAW in September.

In the Chrysler agreement, the union won unprecendented say into future outsourcing decisions made by the automaker. The pact prevents Chrysler Canada from outsourcing work as long as workers are producing a quality profit at a reasonable cost and the company is making a reasonable profit.
GM had argued it required an agreement that was tailored to fit GM's business plan.
Also at issue is GM's decision to sell or close its trim and fabrication plants and outsource other work at a total cost of about 5,500 jobs.
Hargrove said Tuesday the union's most recent position on the bargaining table "would have allowed for the sale of the plants" in return for protection of some of the jobs.
The union leader has said the two sides would need about 72 hours to work out a tentative agreement once talks started again in earnest.
About 26,000 Canadian workers are on strike and the ripple effect of the walkout has idled about 10,000 GM workers in the United States and Mexico.
-- Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100
